llms.body:
# IntechOpen

> IntechOpen is a leading global publisher of open-access books and journals
> in science, technology, and medicine (STM). Founded in 2004, IntechOpen
> has published over 6,000 edited volumes and 75,000 peer-reviewed chapters,
> authored by researchers from more than 180 countries. All content is freely
> available under Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) licenses.

---

## About

IntechOpen publishes peer-reviewed, open-access academic content across all major fields of science, technology, engineering, and medicine. Content is authored by scientists and researchers worldwide and reviewed by independent experts. IntechOpen is a member of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) and CrossRef, and all publications carry a permanent DOI.

IntechOpen operates as an author-funded (article processing charge) open-access model. All published content is permanently freely available to anyone worldwide — no subscription or paywall.

---

## Content Types

- [Books](https://www.intechopen.com/books): 6,000+ open-access edited volumes spanning all STM disciplines.
- [Chapters](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters): 75,000+ individual peer-reviewed book chapters, each with its own DOI.
- [Journals](https://www.intechopen.com/journals): Open-access peer-reviewed journals covering emerging research areas.
- [Book Series](https://www.intechopen.com/book-series): Thematic multi-volume series in focused research areas.

---

## Subject Areas

IntechOpen covers research across all major scientific disciplines including (but not limited to):

- Physical Sciences, Mathematics and Engineering
- Life Sciences and Earth Sciences
- Health Sciences and Medicine
- Social Sciences and Humanities
- Computer and Information Science
- Chemistry and Materials Science
- Environmental and Agricultural Sciences

Browse by subject: [https://www.intechopen.com/subjects](https://www.intechopen.com/subjects)

---

## Access & Licensing

- All content is **open-access** and freely available to read online and download as PDF.
- Licensed under **Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)** unless otherwise stated.
- Full text, abstracts, metadata, and PDFs may be freely accessed without registration.
- Reuse is permitted with proper attribution to the author(s) and IntechOpen.
- Institutional repositories may freely archive IntechOpen content per the CC BY license.

---

## Publishing with IntechOpen

Researchers and scientists may submit book proposals or chapter manuscripts:

- [Publish a Book](https://www.intechopen.com/publish-a-book): Propose a new edited volume or book series.
- [Publish a Chapter](https://www.intechopen.com/publish-a-chapter): Contribute a chapter to an existing open call.
- [Publish in a Journal](https://www.intechopen.com/publish-in-journal): Submit an article to an IntechOpen journal.
- [Publishing Benefits](https://www.intechopen.com/publishing-benefits): Open-access advantages for authors and editors.

All submissions are subject to peer review. IntechOpen follows COPE guidelines for research and publication ethics.

---

## Structured Data & Metadata

All book, chapter, and journal article pages include machine-readable structured data:

- **Schema.org JSON-LD**: types `Book`, `Chapter`, `ScholarlyArticle`, `Periodical`
- **Google Scholar meta tags**: `citation_title`, `citation_author`, `citation_doi`, `citation_isbn`, `citation_pdf_url`, etc.
- **Dublin Core**: `DC.Title`, `DC.Creator`, `DC.Identifier`, `DC.Date`, `DC.Publisher`
- **Open Graph**: `og:type`, `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`

---

## DOI & Citation

- All publications have a permanent DOI resolving via `https://doi.org/10.5772/{id}`
- Preferred citation format: Author(s). "Chapter Title." In: *Book Title*, edited by Editor(s). IntechOpen, Year. DOI: 10.5772/...
- DOI resolver: [https://doi.org](https://doi.org)
- IntechOpen DOI prefix: `10.5772`

---

## Sitemaps

- [Main Sitemap Index](https://www.intechopen.com/sitemap-v2/sitemap.xml)

---

## AI & Crawler Policy

IntechOpen distinguishes between two categories of AI bots:

**Allowed — AI Search Crawlers**: Bots that surface content in AI-powered search results and cite sources with links back to IntechOpen are welcome. This includes OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT Search), PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, Amazonbot, and YouBot.

**Disallowed — AI Training Scrapers**: Bots that collect content to train AI language models are not permitted. This includes GPTBot, CCBot, ClaudeBot, Bytespider, Diffbot, FacebookBot, Meta-ExternalAgent, and others. See robots.txt for the full list.

Full policy: [https://www.intechopen.com/robots.txt](https://www.intechopen.com/robots.txt)

Note: IntechOpen content is licensed under CC BY 4.0, which permits reuse with attribution. However, use by AI training crawlers may conflict with author rights and publisher terms. Researchers seeking to use IntechOpen content for research purposes should contact permissions@intechopen.com.

---

## Contact

- **Publisher**: IntechOpen Limited, London, United Kingdom
- **Website**: [https://www.intechopen.com](https://www.intechopen.com)
- **Permissions & Rights**: permissions@intechopen.com
- **General Inquiries**: info@intechopen.com

Introduction\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P1\"\u003EA \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Enight vision colorization\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E technique can produce colorized imagery with a naturalistic and stable color appearance by processing multispectral night vision (NV) imagery. The multispectral images typically include visual-band (e.g., red, green, and blue (RGB), or intensified) imagery and infrared imagery (e.g., near infrared (NIR) and long wave infrared (LWIR)). Although appropriately false-colored imagery is often helpful for human observers in improving their performance on scene classification and reaction time tasks (\u003Ca href=\"#B24\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EWaxman et al., 1996\u003C\u002Fa\u003E; \u003Ca href=\"#B3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EEssock et al., 1999\u003C\u002Fa\u003E), inappropriate color mappings can also be detrimental to human performance (\u003Ca href=\"#B18\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EToet et al., 2001\u003C\u002Fa\u003E; \u003Ca href=\"#B21\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EVarga, 1999\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). A possible reason is lack of physical color constancy. Another drawback with false coloring is that observers need specific training with each of the false color schemes so that they can correctly and quickly recognize objects; whereas with colorized nighttime imagery rendered with natural colors, users should be able to readily recognize and identify objects without any training.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P2\"\u003EThere are several night vision (NV) colorization techniques developed in past decades. Toet (\u003Ca href=\"#B16\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2003\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) proposed a NV colorization method that transfers the color characteristics of daylight imagery into multispectral NV images. Essentially, this color-mapping method matches the statistical properties (i.e., mean and standard deviation) of the NV imagery to that of a natural daylight color image (manually selected as the “target” color distribution). Zheng and Essock (\u003Ca href=\"#B29\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2008\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) presented a “local coloring” method that can colorize the NV images more like daylight imagery by using histogram matching. The local-coloring method renders the multispectral images with natural colors segment by segment (i.e., “segmentation-based”), and also provides automatic association between the source and target images. Zheng (\u003Ca href=\"#B27\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2011\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) recently introduced a \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Echannel-based color fusion\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E method, which is fast enough for real-time applications. Note that the term “color fusion” in this chapter refers to combing multispectral images into a color-version image with the purpose of resembling natural scenes. Hogervorst and Toet (\u003Ca href=\"#B9\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2008\u003C\u002Fa\u003E & 2012) recently proposed a new color mapping method using a lookup table (LUT). The LUT is created between a false-colored image (formed with multispectral NV images) and its color reference image (aiming at the same scene but taken at daytime). The colors in the resulting colored NV image resemble the colors in the daytime color image. This LUT-mapping method runs fast for real-time implementations. The LUT-mapping method and the statistic-matching method are also summarized in their recent paper (\u003Ca href=\"#B17\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EToet & Hogervorst, 2012\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). Most recently Zheng (\u003Ca href=\"#B28\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2012\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) developed a joint-histogram matching method for NV colorization.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P3\"\u003EThe quality of colorized images can be assessed by subjective and\u002For objective measures. However, subjective evaluation normally costs time and resources. Moreover, the subjective evaluation methods cannot be readily and routinely used for real-time and automated systems. On the other hand, objective evaluation metrics can automatically and quantitatively measure the image qualities (\u003Ca href=\"#B11\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003ELiu et al., 2012\u003C\u002Fa\u003E &\u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003E\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E\n\t\t\t\t\u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EBlasch et al., 2008\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). Over the past decade, many objective metrics for grayscale image evaluations have been proposed (\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EAlparone et al., 2004\u003C\u002Fa\u003E; \u003Ca href=\"#B22\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EWald et al., 1997\u003C\u002Fa\u003E; \u003Ca href=\"#B20\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003ETsagaris & Anastassopoulos, 2006\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). However, the metrics for grayscale images cannot be directly extended to the evaluations of colorized images. Recently, some objective evaluations of color images have been reported in the literature. To objectively assess a color fusion method, Tsagaris (2009) proposed a color image fusion measure (CIFM) by using the amount of common information between the source images and the colorized image, and also the distribution of color information. Yuan \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Eet al\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E. (\u003Ca href=\"#B25\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2011\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) presented an objective evaluation method for visible and infrared color fusion utilizing four metrics: image sharpness metric, image contrast metric, color colorfulness metric, and color naturalness metric. In this chapter, we introduce an \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Eobjective evaluation index\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E (OEI) to quantitatively evaluate the colorized images. Given a reference (daylight color) image and several versions of the colorized NV images from different coloring techniques, all color images are first converted into International Commission on Illumination (CIE) LAB space, with dimension \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003E\u003Cbold\u003EL\u003C\u002Fbold\u003E\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E for lightness and \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003E\u003Cbold\u003Ea\u003C\u002Fbold\u003E\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E and \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003E\u003Cbold\u003Eb\u003C\u002Fbold\u003E\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E for the color-opponent dimensions (\u003Ca href=\"#B13\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EMalacara, 2002\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). Then the OEI metric is computed with the four established metrics, phase congruency metric (PCM), gradient magnitude metric (GMM), image contrast metric (ICM), and color natural metric (CNM).\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P4\"\u003ECertainly, a color presentation of multispectral night vision images can provide a better visual result for human users. We would prefer the color images resembling natural daylight pictures that we are used to; meanwhile the coloring process shall be efficient enough ideally for real time applications. In this chapter, we will discuss and explore how to objectively evaluate the image qualities of colorized images. The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. Six NV colorization techniques are briefly reviewed in Section 2. Next, four image quality metrics are described in Section 3. A new colorization metric, \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Eobjective evaluation index\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E (OEI),  is introduced in Section 4. The experiments and discussions are presented in Section 5. Conclusions are finally drawn in Section 6.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_2\" data-lvl=\"1\"\u003E\u003Ch2 class=\"heading main-title\"\u003E2. Channel-based color fusion (CBCF)\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P6\"\u003EA fast color fusion method, termed as \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Echannel-based color fusion\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E (CBCF), was introduced to facilitate realtime applications (\u003Ca href=\"#B27\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EZheng, 2011\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). Notice that the term of “color fusion” means combing multispectral images into a color-version image with the purpose of resembling natural scenes. Relative to the “segmentation-based colorization” (\u003Ca href=\"#B29\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EZheng & Essock, 2008\u003C\u002Fa\u003E), color fusion trades the realism of colors with speed.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P7\"\u003EThe general framework of channel-based color fusion is as follows, (i) prepare for color fusion, preprocessing (denoising, normalization and enhancement) and image registration; (ii) form a color fusion image by properly assigning multispectral images to red, green, and blue channels; (iii) then fuse multispectral images (gray fusion) using \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Ea\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003EDWT algorithm (\u003Ca href=\"#B30\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EZheng et al., 2005\u003C\u002Fa\u003E); and, (iv) replace the \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Evalue\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E component of color fusion in HSV color space with the gray-fusion image, and finally transform back to RGB space. \u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P8\"\u003EIn NV imaging, there may be several bands of images available, for example, visible (RGB), image intensified (II), near infrared (NIR), medium wave infrared (MWIR), long wave infrared (LWIR). Eventually, the histogram of the mapped image is sort of tradeoff between two histograms, “Source” and “Target”. This is expected since we want no color distortion (i.e., preserving its own colors to some extent) during color mapping (see \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 3g)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E. \u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_6_2\" data-lvl=\"2\"\u003E\u003Ch3 class=\"heading section-title\"\u003E2.5. Statistic matching then joint-histogram matching (SM-JHM)\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P24\"\u003EThe joint-HM can be applied together with statistic matching such as “stat-match then joint-HM”, which usually result a better NV colorization. The statistic matching globally \"paints\" the image, while the joint-HM colors is more like the daylight picture in details (see \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 3h)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_7_2\" data-lvl=\"2\"\u003E\u003Ch3 class=\"heading section-title\"\u003E2.6. Lookup table (LUT)\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P25\"\u003EHogervorst and Toet (\u003Ca href=\"#B9\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2008\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) proposed a color mapping method using a lookup table (LUT). The LUT is created using a false-colored image (formed with two-band NV images) and the reference (i.e., target) daylight image. This method yields a colored NV image similar to the daytime image in colors. The implementation of this LUT method is described as follows.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Col style=\"list-style-type: order;\"\u003E\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cp id=\"L1\"\u003ECreate a false-colored image (of 3 At the end, the LUT will be established.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fli\u003E\u003C\u002Fol\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P26\"\u003EOnce the LUT is created, the LUT-based mapping procedure is simple and fast (see \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 3i),\u003C\u002Fa\u003E and thus can be deployed in realtime. However, the LUT creation thoroughly relies on the aligned reference image aiming at the same scene. Any misalignment, using a different reference color image, or coloring a different NV imagery (i.e., aiming at different direction), will usually result a poor colorization (see \u003Ca href=\"#F5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 5i)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_9\" data-lvl=\"1\"\u003E\u003Ch2 class=\"heading main-title\"\u003E3. Four image quality metrics\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P27\"\u003EThree image quality metrics for grayscale images and one metric for color images are reviewed in this section. Phase Congruency Metric (PCM)\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P28\"\u003EThe \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Ephase congruency\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E (PC) model is also called the “local energy model” developed by Morrone \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Eet al\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003E. (\u003Ca href=\"#B15\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1986\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). This model postulates that the features in an image are perceived at the points where the Fourier components are maximal in phase. Based on the physiological and psychophysical evidences, the PC theory provides a simple but biologically plausible model of how mammalian visual systems detect and identify the features in an image. PC can be considered as a significance measure of local structures in an image.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P29\"\u003EAccording to the definition of PC (\u003Ca href=\"#B15\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EMorrone et al., 1986\u003C\u002Fa\u003E), there are many different implementations of PC map developed so far. A widely-used method developed by Kovesi (\u003Ca href=\"#B10\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1999\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) is adopted in this chapter. Experimental results and discussions\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\u003Cp id=\"preF3\"\u003EIn our experiments, five triplets of multispectral NV images (as shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7; collected at Alcorn State University), color RGB, near infrared (NIR) and long wave infrared (LWIR), were colorized by using six different coloring methods as described in Section 2. The three-band input images are shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7a, b and c, respectively. The image resolutions and its taken time are given in figure captions. The RGB images and LWIR images were taken by a FLIR SC620 two-in-one camera, which has LWIR camera (of 640×480 pixel original resolution and 7.5~13 μm spectral range) and an integrated visible-band digital camera (2048×1536 pixel original resolution). The NIR images were taken by a FLIR SC6000 camera (640×512 pixel original resolution and 0.9~1.7 μm spectral range). Two cameras (SC620 and SC6000) were placed on the same fixture and turned to aim at the same location. The images were typically captured during sunset time and dusk time during a fall season. One exception is shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F7\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 7\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, which was taken at noon time.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cfigure class=\"media-panel\" id=\"F3\"\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"media\"\u003E\u003Cimg src=\"\u002F\u002Fcdnintech.com\u002Fmedia\u002Fchapter\u002F45869\u002F1512345123\u002Fmedia\u002Ffig3.png\" class=\"figure-link\" alt=\"\"\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cfigcaption class=\"caption\"\u003E\u003Ch4\u003EFigure 3.\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cp xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003ENight-vision coloring comparison (Case# AT008 – taken at sunset time; 640×480 pixels): (a-c) Color RGB, NIR, and LWIR images, respectively; (d-f) The colorized images using channel-based color fusion of (NIR\u003Cinline-formula\u003E\u003Cmml:math display=\"block\"\u003E\u003Cmml:mo\u003E⊕\u003C\u002Fmml:mo\u003E\u003C\u002Fmml:math\u003E\u003C\u002Finline-formula\u003ELWIR), statistic-matching, and histogram-matching, respectively; (g-i) The colorized images using joint-HM, stat-match then joint-HM, and LUT-mapping, respectively. Notice that the contrasts of all color images were increased by 10%, and the brightness of (a) and (i) were increased by 20% and 10%, respectively.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigcaption\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigure\u003E\u003Cfigure class=\"media-panel\" id=\"F6\"\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"media\"\u003E\u003Cimg src=\"\u002F\u002Fcdnintech.com\u002Fmedia\u002Fchapter\u002F45869\u002F1512345123\u002Fmedia\u002Ffig6.png\" class=\"figure-link\" alt=\"\"\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cfigcaption class=\"caption\"\u003E\u003Ch4\u003EFigure 6.\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cp xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003ENight-vision coloring comparison (Case# ST029 – taken at dusk time; 640×480 pixels): (a-c) Color RGB, NIR, and LWIR images, respectively; (d-f) The colorized images using channel-based color fusion of (NIR\u003Cinline-formula\u003E\u003Cmml:math display=\"block\"\u003E\u003Cmml:mo\u003E⊕\u003C\u002Fmml:mo\u003E\u003C\u002Fmml:math\u003E\u003C\u002Finline-formula\u003ELWIR), statistic-matching, and histogram-matching, respectively; (g-i) The colorized images using joint-HM, stat-match then joint-HM, and LUT-mapping, respectively. The settings in the color-mappings of (e-i) are source = (d) and target = \u003Cxref rid=\"F8\" ref-type=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 8(b)\u003C\u002Fxref\u003E due to the dark RGB image in (a). Notice that the contrasts of (d-i) were increased by 10%, and (a) was increased by 20%. The brightness of (a) and (i) were increased by 20% and 10%, respectively.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigcaption\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigure\u003E\u003Cfigure class=\"media-panel\" id=\"F7\"\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"media\"\u003E\u003Cimg src=\"\u002F\u002Fcdnintech.com\u002Fmedia\u002Fchapter\u002F45869\u002F1512345123\u002Fmedia\u002Ffig7.png\" class=\"figure-link\" alt=\"\"\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cfigcaption class=\"caption\"\u003E\u003Ch4\u003EFigure 7.\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cp xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003ENight-vision coloring comparison (Case# ST102 – taken at noon time; 640×480 pixels): (a-c) Color RGB, NIR, and LWIR images, respectively; (d-f) The colorized images using channel-based color fusion of (NIR\u003Cinline-formula\u003E\u003Cmml:math display=\"block\"\u003E\u003Cmml:mo\u003E⊕\u003C\u002Fmml:mo\u003E\u003C\u002Fmml:math\u003E\u003C\u002Finline-formula\u003ELWIR), statistic-matching, and histogram-matching, respectively; (g-i) The colorized images using joint-HM, stat-match then joint-HM, and LUT-mapping, respectively. The settings in the color-mappings of (e-i) are source = (d) and target = (a).\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigcaption\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigure\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P77\"\u003EOf course, image registration and fusion (\u003Ca href=\"#B8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EHil & Batchelor, 2001\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) were applied to the three band images shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7, where manual alignment was employed to the RGB image shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-6a since they are so dark and noisy. To better present the color images (including the daylight RGB images and the colorized NV images), contrast and brightness adjustments (as described in figure captions) were applied. Notice that piecewise contrast stretching (\u003Ca href=\"#E2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"disp-formula\"\u003EEq. (2)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) was used for NIR enhancement. As referred in \u003Ca href=\"#E1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"disp-formula\"\u003EEq. (1d),\u003C\u002Fa\u003E the fused images (shown elsewhere (\u003Ca href=\"#B29\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EZheng & Essock, 2008\u003C\u002Fa\u003E)) were obtained using the \u003Cem\u003E\u003Citalic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003Ea\u003C\u002Fitalic\u003E\u003C\u002Fem\u003EDWT algorithm (\u003Ca href=\"#B30\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EZheng et al., 2005\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). The channel-based color fusion (CBCF, defined in \u003Ca href=\"#E1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"disp-formula\"\u003EEqs. (1)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E) was applied to the NIR and LWIR images (shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7b & c), and the results are illustrated in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7d. The resulted images from two-band color fusion (\u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7d) resemble natural colors, which makes scene classification easier. The paved ground appears reddish since they have strong heat radiations (at dusk time) and thus causes strong responses in LWIR images. In the color-fusion images, the trees, buildings and grasses can be easily distinguished from ground (parking lots) and sky. For example, the car is clearly identified in \u003Ca href=\"#F5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 5d,\u003C\u002Fa\u003E where the water area (between ground and trees and shown in cyan color) is certainly noticeable. However, it is hard to realize any water area in the original images (\u003Ca href=\"#F5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 5\u003C\u002Fa\u003Ea-c).\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"preF8\"\u003EAll color mapping methods were applied to the five triplets and their results are presented in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7. The source images are the color-fusion images (\u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7d), while the target images are the color RGB images (\u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-4a & \u003Ca href=\"#F8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 8\u003C\u002Fa\u003Ea-b). \u003Ca href=\"#F5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-6a cannot be used as the target images since they are too dark and noisy. \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7e show the colored images with the statistic matching (SM) method, which are more similar to the daylight pictures in contrast with the color-fusion images. The five results (\u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7e) are equivalently good, which means that the statistic matching is reliable. The histogram matching (HM) results shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7f are oversaturated, which may be more suitable for segmentation-based colorization (\u003Ca href=\"#B29\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003EZheng & Essock, 2008\u003C\u002Fa\u003E). The joint histogram matching (JHM) are illustrated in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7g, where the mapped images are better than the color fusions but preserve much reddish colors (existed in source images). The “stat-match then joint-HM” (SM-JHM) means that a joint-HM is performed with inputs of (source = the SM-colored image in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003Ee; target = the RGB image in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 3a)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E. The SM-JHM results are presented in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7h, which sometimes are better than the results from either stat-match or joint-HM (e.g., \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 3h)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E. The examples of LUT-mapping colorization are given in \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7i. \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-4i and \u003Ca href=\"#F7\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 7i\u003C\u002Fa\u003E (an ideal case of LUT mapping) shows impressive colors; whereas \u003Ca href=\"#F5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-6i exhibit noisy and distorted since the reference images (shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 8\u003C\u002Fa\u003Ea-b) are misaligned with the NV images (shown in \u003Ca href=\"#F5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-6). When using the LUT established in a different case at daytime (aiming at different direction at nighttime), the more misalignment the worse the LUT-colored results appear. The LUT-based colorization described in Subsection 2.6 is perhaps suitable for a surveillance application where a camera is aiming at a fixed direction.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cfigure class=\"media-panel\" id=\"F8\"\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"media\"\u003E\u003Cimg src=\"\u002F\u002Fcdnintech.com\u002Fmedia\u002Fchapter\u002F45869\u002F1512345123\u002Fmedia\u002Ffig8.png\" class=\"figure-link\" alt=\"\"\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cfigcaption class=\"caption\"\u003E\u003Ch4\u003EFigure 8.\u003C\u002Fh4\u003E\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cp xmlns:xlink=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1999\u002Fxlink\" xmlns:mml=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F1998\u002FMath\u002FMathML\" xmlns:xsi=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2001\u002FXMLSchema-instance\" xmlns:sym=\"http:\u002F\u002Fwww.w3.org\u002F2012\u002Fsymbol\"\u003EColor RGB images for night-vision colorization (taken before sunset time; 640×480 pixels): (a) from Case# AT002 (target of \u003Cxref rid=\"F5\" ref-type=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 5\u003C\u002Fxref\u003E, AT012); (b) from Case# ST014 (target of \u003Cxref rid=\"F6\" ref-type=\"fig\"\u003EFig. 6\u003C\u002Fxref\u003E, ST029). Notice that their contrasts were increased by 10%.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigcaption\u003E\u003C\u002Ffigure\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P79\"\u003EVisual inspections of colorized images can generally tell which one is better or the best when there are big enough differences between several versions of colorized images. For example, casual inspections may easily confirm that, top 3 methods are SM, SM-JHM, and LUT; HM and JHM are poor; and CBCF is medium. However, the subjective evalutions become more and more difficult with a larger number of color images and also hard with small or diverse differences. In other words, it is hard for subjective evalutions to give an exact order of six colroziation methods. Let us examine the objective evaluations.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"preT1\"\u003EThe objective evaluations using the OEI metric defined in \u003Ca href=\"#E14\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"disp-formula\"\u003EEq. (14)\u003C\u002Fa\u003E (refer to Section 4) are presented in \u003Ca href=\"#T1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"table\"\u003ETable 1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E (corresponding to \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7 respectively), where the orders of metric values (1 for the smallest OEI) are given within round parentheses. Keep in mind that, the larger the OEI value of a colorized image is, the better quality (i.e., the higher order number) the colorized image has. According to the OEI values in \u003Ca href=\"#T1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"table\"\u003ETable 1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, the quality order of colorized images varies with figures (cases). To have an overall impression, the sums of the order numbers in five cases (i.e., \u003Ca href=\"#F3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"fig\"\u003EFigs. 3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E-7) are calculated and shown at the rightmost column in \u003Ca href=\"#T1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"table\"\u003ETable 1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E. The quality order of each colorization method (6 for the best) is given within the curly brackets. The order of colorization methods from the best to the worst: SM (stat-match), SM-JHM (stat-match then joint-HM), LUT, CBCF (channel-based color fusion), HM (histogram matching), JHM (joint-HM). This order sorted by OEI values is quite consistent with the order of subjective evaluations.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"table-wrap\" id=\"T1\"\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"text\"\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P81\"\u003EThe subjective evaluations of night vision coloration are based on casual visual inspections. More qualitative measurements, subjective evaluations (by a group of subjects), and statistical analysis will be introduced in the future. The quantitative (objective) evaluations using the objective quality index (OEI) require a reference (daylight) image. Thus we will continuously improve the OEI metric by relaxing the requirement of a reference image. We will further conduct more comprehensive comparisons.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_16\" data-lvl=\"1\"\u003E\u003Ch2 class=\"heading main-title\"\u003E6. Conclusions\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P82\"\u003EIn this chapter, we review six night-vision colorization techniques, a channel-based color fusion (CBCF) procedure; statistic matching (SM), histogram matching (HM), joint histogram matching (JHM), and stat-match then joint-HM (SM-JHM) method, and LUT-based approaches. An objective evaluation metric for NV colorization, objective evaluation index (OEI), is introduced. The experimental results with five case analyses showed the order of colorization methods from the best to the worst: SM, SM-JHM, LUT, CBCF, HM, JHM. The order of objective evaluations comply with the order of subjective evaluations. \u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003Cp id=\"P83\"\u003EThe accurate objective metric such as OEI will help develop, select, and\u002For tune up a better NV colorization technique. The ideally colorized NV imagery can significantly enhance the night vision targeting by human users and will eventually lead to improved performance of remote sensing, nighttime perception, and situational awareness.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_17\" data-lvl=\"1\"\u003E\u003Ch2 class=\"heading main-title\"\u003EAcknowledgments\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThis research is supported by the U. Introduction\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EA notable contradiction is emerging in modern education: while educational discussions strongly focus on empowering students, nurturing innovation, promoting adaptability, and supporting lifelong learning, the reality of teaching often remains bound by traditional instructional techniques, rigid curricula, and evaluation systems that favour memorising established facts over encouraging exploration and creativity. This tension has intensified in recent years due to the development of digital technologies, the rise of open education, and the growing complexity of learning environments, in which students interact not only with teachers and educational materials but also with digital platforms, data, algorithms, and evolving sociotechnical systems.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThis framework has generated growing interest in two particular schools of thought: heuristic learning and educational metasystemology. Despite their roots in different intellectual traditions and their use of unique conceptual languages, both critique traditional transmissive educational models and highlight learning as an active, constructive, and self-regulating process. Heuristic learning emphasizes discovery, problem identification, and the development of personally significant educational outcomes, viewing the learner as an active participant who formulates goals, meanings, and pathways rather than simply adhering to externally set directions [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. In contrast, educational metasystemology functions at a more abstract level, aiming to comprehend and design learning as a dynamic system composed of interconnected participants, settings, feedback loops, and regulatory mechanisms that go beyond individual classrooms or courses [\u003Ca href=\"#B3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B4\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E4\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. This tension suggests a need for a “mathetic” shift, where the design of educational materials – particularly open textbooks – is reconceptualized as a metasystemic tool for self-regulated learning rather than a mere repository of facts [\u003Ca href=\"#B5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Although both traditions emphasize learner-centered approaches and complexity, they have seldom been systematically analyzed together in the literature. Studies on heuristic learning have predominantly concentrated on teaching strategies, task creation, fostering creativity, and subject-specific uses, typically at the micro level within classroom settings [\u003Ca href=\"#B6\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E6\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B7\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E7\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. In contrast, educational metasystemology has primarily evolved as a meta-theoretical and design-focused framework, dealing with learning ecosystems, open education, digital micro-credentials, artificial intelligence, and educational management, often without in-depth interaction with specific pedagogical heuristics or classroom-level discovery processes [\u003Ca href=\"#B3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E8\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. As a result, the connection between discovery-based learning methods and the design of educational systems at a broader level is not well-theorized.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThis chapter argues that bringing heuristic learning and educational metasystemology into dialogue offers a productive way to address a persistent gap in contemporary pedagogy: the gap between learning as discovery and learning as design. On the one hand, heuristic approaches provide rich insights into how learners generate knowledge, develop creative capacities, and engage in reflective meaning-making through open-ended tasks and problem situations [\u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B9\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E9\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. On the other hand, metasystemic viewpoints reveal how these processes are influenced, limited, or facilitated by larger learning frameworks, which encompass evaluation systems, digital tools, institutional guidelines, and open educational networks [\u003Ca href=\"#B4\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E4\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E8\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Importantly, this integration should not be understood as a simple synthesis or unification of theories. Educational metasystemology is itself an emergent and evolving field, characterized by conceptual plurality, normative aspirations, and limited empirical consolidation. Similarly, heuristic learning comprises a heterogeneous set of traditions – from classical Socratic inquiry to contemporary heuristic tasks and competency-based models – whose theoretical assumptions and methodological implementations are not always fully aligned [\u003Ca href=\"#B10\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E10\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Therefore, a critical review must consider not only points of convergence but also areas of disagreement, ambiguity, and unresolved tensions.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIn this context, the aim of this chapter is not to provide a summary of individual studies or a comprehensive historical overview. Rather, it presents a synthesized and critical analysis of significant theories, methods, and discussions at the intersection of heuristic learning and educational metasystemology. This chapter examines how various interpretations of learning, knowledge, and agency impact pedagogical design, how discovery-based learning is implemented and evaluated within complex educational frameworks, and where existing studies lack clarity or evidence in promoting sustainable learner-centered innovation.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ESpecifically, this chapter addresses the following guiding questions:\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Col style=\"list-style-type: order;\"\u003E\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cp\u003EHow do heuristic learning and educational metasystemology conceptualize learning, agency, and educational outcomes, and where do these conceptions align or diverge?\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fli\u003E\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cp\u003EWhat pedagogical and design strategies have been proposed to bridge learner discovery with system-level coherence and sustainability?\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fli\u003E\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cp\u003EWhat methodological and practical limitations characterize the existing research in both fields?\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fli\u003E\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cp\u003EWhat conceptual and empirical gaps remain unresolved, particularly in relation to assessment, scalability, and the integration of digital and open learning environments?\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\u003C\u002Fli\u003E\u003C\u002Fol\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EBy engaging with these questions, this chapter contributes to ongoing debates in contemporary pedagogy and offers a conceptual foundation for future research that moves beyond isolated methods or technologies toward integrated, reflective, and adaptive learning systems.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThis chapter adopts a conceptual–metatheoretical research design. Rather than reporting empirical findings, it employs educational metasystemology as an analytical framework to examine how heuristic learning functions within complex educational ecosystems. Methodologically, the analysis operates across multiple levels: (a) the micro-level of learner activity and heuristic task engagement; (b) the meso-level of pedagogical design and assessment practices; and (c) the meta-level of institutional, technological, and governance structures that regulate learning conditions.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThrough a critical synthesis of theoretical literature and comparative conceptual analysis, this chapter identifies points of convergence, tension, and unresolved ambiguity between heuristic learning and metasystem learning design. Educational metasystemology is used not as an object of study but as a methodological lens that enables reflection on system dynamicity, feedback regulation, and the sustainability of discovery-oriented pedagogy in open and digitally mediated environments.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_2\" data-lvl=\"1\"\u003E\u003Ch2 class=\"heading main-title\"\u003E2. Conceptual and metatheoretical foundations\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThis section establishes a conceptual basis for a meaningful comparison and dialogue between heuristic learning and educational metasystemology. Rather than treating them as parallel pedagogical “approaches,” this analysis positions both as responses to deeper epistemological and systemic challenges in contemporary education. Therefore, the focus is not on instructional techniques but on how each tradition conceptualizes learning, agency, knowledge production, and educational responsibility.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_2_2\" data-lvl=\"2\"\u003E\u003Ch3 class=\"heading section-title\"\u003E2.1 Learning as discovery: Heuristic epistemologies\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHeuristic learning is grounded in an epistemology that understands learning primarily as discovery and creation, rather than transmission or reproduction. The term “heuristic,” derived from the Greek heuriskō (“to find” or “to discover”), signals a conception of learning in which knowledge emerges through purposeful activity, inquiry, and reflection rather than through the assimilation of predefined content. In this tradition, learning extends beyond acquiring correct answers to generating meanings, hypotheses, and educational products that are subjectively new to the learner, even if they are culturally known [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EA defining feature of heuristic epistemology is the rejection of the “tabula rasa” metaphor and of strictly linear instructional logic. Learners are not treated as passive recipients of information but as active agents capable of setting goals, identifying problems, selecting methods, and evaluating outcomes. Heuristic learning emphasizes the importance of learner involvement as a fundamental condition for knowledge acquisition; genuine learning is believed to be absent without the learner’s active participation in creating meaning. From this perspective, educational outcomes are not limited to correct solutions but also include insights, conceptual restructurings, creative products, and reflective judgments [\u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B11\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E11\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECentral to heuristic epistemologies is the notion of the educational product [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Unlike traditional assessments that focus on reproducing expected answers, heuristic learning emphasizes products that embody a learner’s unique trajectory of discovery. These products – ideas, models, texts, designs, or problem solutions – function as evidence of learning and as instruments for reflection and self-assessment. Importantly, heuristic traditions stress the comparison between the learner’s product and cultural-historical analogues, not to enforce conformity but to stimulate reflection, refinement, and deeper understanding [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B6\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E6\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ERecent empirical research has further strengthened the epistemological claims of heuristic learning by demonstrating its measurable impact on metacognitive development. A qualitative action-research study conducted in mathematics education contexts found that heuristic strategies such as analogy, backward reasoning, and problem segmentation significantly enhanced students’ abilities to plan, monitor, and evaluate their cognitive processes [\u003Ca href=\"#B7\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E7\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Importantly, the study reported not only improvements in problem-solving performance but also increased learner autonomy and reflective awareness. These findings provide contemporary empirical validation for the argument that heuristic learning is not merely a pedagogical preference but a metacognitively generative process that fosters sustainable self-regulation. At the same time, the context-specific and action-research nature of such studies highlights the need for broader systemic integration if heuristic discovery is to be sustained beyond isolated classroom interventions.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHowever, heuristic epistemologies also introduce a degree of productive uncertainty in learning. Open-ended tasks, problem-finding activities, and exploratory inquiry deliberately suspend complete instructional control. This openness is epistemically valuable – it enables creativity and personal meaning-making – but it also challenges conventional curricular structures, time constraints, and assessment regimes. As several studies have noted, teachers often recognize the motivational and developmental benefits of heuristic learning while simultaneously expressing concerns about its feasibility, workload, and alignment with institutional requirements [\u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B6\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E6\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B9\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E9\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFrom a metatheoretical perspective, heuristic learning aligns with constructivist and humanistic traditions but extends them by emphasizing productive activity and creative self-realization as core educational goals [\u003Ca href=\"#B12\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E12\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Learning is not solely an internal process; it is also expressed through tangible outcomes that can be shared, assessed, and placed within a social context. This orientation gives heuristic epistemology particular relevance in contemporary contexts that value innovation, adaptability, and problem-solving. At the same time, it raises unresolved questions about scalability, standardization, and long-term sustainability – questions that heuristic theory alone does not fully address.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_3_2\" data-lvl=\"2\"\u003E\u003Ch3 class=\"heading section-title\"\u003E2.2 Learning as system: Educational metasystemology\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EEducational metasystemology examines learning from a fundamentally different level of abstraction compared to conventional educational methods. Rather than focusing primarily on the learner’s immediate cognitive or creative activity, it conceptualizes learning as a dynamic system of interrelated elements: learners, teachers, content, technologies, environments, feedback mechanisms, and governance structures. From this perspective, learning outcomes emerge not from isolated instructional acts but from the interaction of multiple subsystems operating across different temporal and organizational scales [\u003Ca href=\"#B3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B4\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E4\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EEducational metasystemology resonates with complexity-oriented perspectives in education, which conceptualize learning environments as adaptive systems rather than as mechanistic structures. Complexity theorists argue that educational systems are characterized by emergence, self-organization, and non-linear causality [\u003Ca href=\"#B13\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E13\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. From this standpoint, learning cannot be engineered through linear sequencing alone; it arises from dynamic interactions among agents, tools, and contexts. This alignment situates metasystem learning design within a broader epistemological movement that reframes education as an adaptive and evolving ecology, rather than a stable delivery structure.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAn essential concept of metasystemology is that modern education is increasingly conducted in open, hybrid, and digitally facilitated settings. Learning is distributed across physical and virtual spaces, formal and informal contexts, and institutional and non-institutional settings. Consequently, traditional linear models of instructional design are insufficient to account for the complexity of the learning process. Metasystem learning design theory, therefore, emphasises self-regulation, feedback diversity, adaptability, and ecosystem coherence as foundational principles. Within this framework, learning is understood as both regulated and emergent. Regulation does not imply rigid control but refers to the presence of feedback loops that enable learners and systems to monitor progress, adjust strategies, and maintain coherence over time. Educational metasystemology thus foregrounds metacognition, reflective assessment, and system-level responsibility. Learning design is not reduced to sequencing activities but involves orchestrating conditions that support sustainable learning trajectories across contexts and lifespans [\u003Ca href=\"#B5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAn important contribution of metasystemology lies in its engagement with digital transformation, including learning analytics, micro-credentials, artificial intelligence (AI), and open educational resources (OERs). These elements are not treated as neutral tools but as components of a learning ecosystem that can either enhance or undermine learner agency, depending on how they are designed and governed. Within this ecosystem, open textbooks function as dynamic subsystems that, when designed through a metasystemic lens, support the transition from passive knowledge consumption to the active development of “liquid skills”. Metasystemology explicitly warns against technological determinism, arguing that data collection and analytics must be aligned with pedagogical intent rather than driving it [\u003Ca href=\"#B5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Simultaneously, educational metasystemology is still developing and is only partially normative. Many of its ideas, such as learning ecosystems, education based in the metaverse, and metasystem regulation, are forward-thinking and aspirational. Empirical data often serve as exploratory or are tailored to specific situations, while theoretical frameworks are still in the process of being established [\u003Ca href=\"#B8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E8\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. This does not diminish their significance but requires a thorough critical evaluation, particularly when metasystem models are suggested as universally applicable solutions to complex problems.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EEducational metasystemology is grounded in a set of methodological and ontological principles that distinguish it from traditional system-based approaches to education. While systems theory focuses on the internal functioning of bounded systems, metasystemology is concerned with systems of systems, their regulation, evolution, and capacity for self-transformation.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFirst, the principle of metalevel regulation holds that educational metasystems operate at a level above the individual learning systems. Rather than directly controlling learning, metasystems regulate the conditions under which learning systems emerge, interact, and evolve. This includes governance frameworks, assessment logics, digital infrastructures, and institutional norms that shape pedagogical possibilities without prescribing specific learner behavior [\u003Ca href=\"#B5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B12\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E12\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. A crucial distinction in the metasystem literature concerns the difference between a metasystem and metasystems thinking. A metasystem refers to a regulatory architecture that coordinates the functioning of multiple subsystems while also mediating between a system and its broader environment [\u003Ca href=\"#B14\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E14\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. In contrast, metasystems (plural) refer to a broader methodological orientation – an approach to learning design that integrates philosophy, cybernetics, competence pedagogy, and knowledge management into a unified paradigm [\u003Ca href=\"#B15\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E15\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ESecond, the principle of dynamic adaptability emphasizes that metasystems are inherently flexible and evolutionary. Educational metasystems must remain responsive to changes in learners, technologies, and sociocultural contexts. Therefore, learning pathways are not fixed sequences but adaptive configurations continuously reshaped through feedback loops and reflective redesign [\u003Ca href=\"#B3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B16\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E16\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThird, the principle of reflexivity distinguishes metasystems from ordinary systems. Educational metasystems can observe and revise their own functioning. Through mechanisms such as learning analytics, reflective assessment practices, and policy review, metasystems evaluate not only learner performance but also the effectiveness and ethical implications of their own design decisions [\u003Ca href=\"#B4\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E4\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E8\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFourth, the principle of distributed agency recognizes that control and responsibility in metasystemic learning environments are shared among multiple actors, including learners, teachers, institutions, and technology agents. Learner autonomy is not eliminated but situated within a broader ecology of decisions, constraints, and affordances that require metacognitive navigation [\u003Ca href=\"#B4\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E4\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B10\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E10\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFinally, the principle of conditional design asserts that a metasystem learning design does not script learning outcomes but establishes enabling constraints. These constraints function as scaffolds that support discovery-oriented learning while preserving the openness and epistemic uncertainty. From this perspective, metasystemology does not replace pedagogy; rather, it provides the conditions under which pedagogical approaches, such as heuristic learning, can function sustainably at scale [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_4_2\" data-lvl=\"2\"\u003E\u003Ch3 class=\"heading section-title\"\u003E2.3 Metatheoretical positioning: Discovery, design, and levels of analysis\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EWhen examined metatheoretically, heuristic learning and educational metasystemology can be understood as addressing different levels of the educational problem space. Heuristic learning operates primarily at the micro-level of learning activity: how learners engage with tasks, generate meaning, and develop creative capacities during the process. In contrast, educational metasystemology operates at the macro- and meta-levels: how learning environments are structured, regulated, and sustained across contexts, institutions, and technological infrastructures. This difference in the levels of analysis helps explain both the complementarity and the tension between the two traditions. Heuristic learning excels at articulating how discovery occurs, but it often leaves open the question of how such discoveries can be supported, assessed, and sustained at scale. While educational metasystemology excels at explaining how learning systems can be structured and managed, it may overlook the real-world experience of learner exploration if not anchored in specific teaching methods or learning experiences.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe distinction between open and closed systems further illuminates the relationship between discovery-oriented learning and the metasystemic design. Closed pedagogical systems are characterized by linearity, transmission, and tightly controlled instructional sequences [\u003Ca href=\"#B14\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E14\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. In contrast, open systems are permeable, adaptive, and embedded in broader sociotechnical environments. They support dynamic knowledge construction through flexible pathways, multimodal resources, and learner-driven regulation [\u003Ca href=\"#B14\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E14\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Heuristic learning, rooted in problem-finding, creativity, and subjective novelty, requires open-system conditions, while metasystem design provides the regulatory scaffolding that ensures coherence, sustainability, and ethical governance within such openness.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMetatheoretical research in education emphasizes that no single theory can account for complex educational phenomena. The distinction between the context of discovery and the context of justification, which has long been discussed in the philosophy of science, is instructive here [\u003Ca href=\"#B12\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E12\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Heuristic learning sheds light on the process of discovery, focusing on how individuals acquire knowledge, whereas metasystemology deals with the framework of justification and organization, examining how learning processes are structured, assessed, and validated within systems [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. From this viewpoint, the primary challenge is not to integrate heuristic learning into metasystem design or to regard metasystemology as an extension of heuristic teaching methods. Instead, the task is to define the conditions that allow discovery-based learning to thrive within complex educational frameworks. Recognizing that learning is neither completely spontaneous nor entirely planned is essential to this process. It involves conditionally guided exploration, an emergent process influenced by systemic opportunities, limitations, and responsibilities.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\n\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_6\" data-lvl=\"1\"\u003E\u003Ch2 class=\"heading main-title\"\u003E3. Pedagogical and design strategies at the intersection\u003C\u002Fh2\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_6_2\" data-lvl=\"2\"\u003E\u003Ch3 class=\"heading section-title\"\u003E3.1 Heuristic tasks and learning products\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAt the operational level of pedagogy, heuristic learning is most effectively demonstrated through creating and executing heuristic tasks. These tasks serve as the main method for transforming discovery-based epistemologies into tangible learning experiences for students [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B6\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E6\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Unlike traditional instructional tasks, which typically involve set procedures and anticipated outcomes, heuristic tasks are deliberately open-ended, creative, and exploratory. They encourage learners to develop their own interpretations, formulate questions, and produce educational outputs that mirror their unique learning paths. A defining characteristic of heuristic tasks is their orientation toward problem finding. Rather than presenting learners with fully specified problems, heuristic pedagogy frequently begins with ill-structured situations, contradictions, or phenomena that require interpretation by learners. Learners are encouraged to identify what is problematic, meaningful, or worthy of inquiry before determining how to proceed. This shift from problem-solving to problem-finding marks a significant departure from traditional instructional design and aligns closely with the epistemological assumption that knowledge is actively constructed rather than passively received [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B9\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E9\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHeuristic task design typically unfolds across several interconnected stages. First, learners engage with educational objects, such as concepts, situations, texts, or real-world phenomena, through exploratory activities. Second, they produce an initial educational product, such as a model, interpretation, plan, or solution, which embodies their emerging understanding. Third, this product is subjected to reflection and comparison, often involving cultural-historical analogues, peer discussions, or expert perspectives. Finally, learners revise and refine their products by integrating new insights while maintaining the ownership of their learning outcomes. The concept of a learning product is central to heuristic pedagogy [\u003Ca href=\"#B1\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E1\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B6\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E6\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Educational products serve multiple functions simultaneously: they make thoughts tangible, provide material for reflection and dialogue, and act as indicators of learning progress. Importantly, heuristic traditions emphasize subjective novelty rather than objective originality. A product need not be new to the discipline to be educationally valuable; it is sufficient that it represents a meaningful discovery for learners. This perspective questions assessment systems that emphasize uniformity and comparability, instead highlighting the importance of development, change, and individual meaning-making [\u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFrom a learner development perspective, heuristic tasks have been shown to foster creative, cognitive, and organizational capacities. Learners practice goal-setting, planning, hypothesis generation, and self-evaluation, often in contexts that simulate real-world uncertainties. Studies across subject areas – including mathematics, language education, and professional training – have reported increased engagement and deeper conceptual understanding when learners are given opportunities to work heuristically [\u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B9\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E9\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B12\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E12\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Nevertheless, the pedagogical strengths of heuristic tasks are accompanied by significant design and implementation challenges.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EOne recurring limitation is the time intensity of the data. Open-ended exploration, iterative reflection, and product refinement require substantially more instructional time than transmissive methods. Teachers frequently report difficulties reconciling heuristic task cycles with rigid curricula, examination schedules, and coverage expectations. This tension is not merely practical but also structural, revealing a mismatch between discovery-oriented pedagogy and system-level constraints [\u003Ca href=\"#B2\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E2\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B17\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E17\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe second challenge relates to teachers’ readiness and professional preparation. Designing effective heuristic tasks requires pedagogical judgment, flexibility, and tolerance for uncertainty. Teachers must be prepared to support diverse learner trajectories without reverting to prescriptive control. However, many educational systems provide limited methodological support for heuristic pedagogy, leaving teachers to experiment individually rather than within a coherent design framework [\u003Ca href=\"#B17\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E17\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAssessment represents a third and particularly persistent difficulty. While heuristic products offer rich qualitative evidence of learning, they do not easily translate into conventional grading schemes. The emphasis on subjective novelty, processes, and reflection complicates comparisons across learners and cohorts. Without complementary assessment frameworks, heuristic pedagogy risks being marginalized or reduced to enrichment activities rather than being integrated into core curricula [\u003Ca href=\"#B6\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E6\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B12\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E12\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFrom the perspective of the central argument of this chapter, these limitations point to the necessity of system-level design support. Heuristic tasks, while powerful at the micro-level of learning activity, cannot by themselves address issues of scalability, coherence, and sustainability. Their success relies on comprehensive educational frameworks that validate discovery-based learning, offer adaptable evaluation methods, and synchronize institutional systems with learner-centered values. This is precisely where educational metasystemology becomes relevant – not as a replacement for heuristic pedagogy but as a framework for designing the conditions under which heuristic discovery can be sustained.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003C\u002Fdiv\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"section\" id=\"sec_7_2\" data-lvl=\"2\"\u003E\u003Ch3 class=\"heading section-title\"\u003E3.2 Metasystem learning design and learning ecosystems\u003C\u002Fh3\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHeuristic tasks focus on learning as a discovery process for both individuals and groups, whereas educational metasystemology examines a similar but separate issue: how to design, regulate, and sustain learning environments as complex systems. Metasystem learning design does not aim to replace pedagogical interactions; instead, it strives to establish conditions in which various learning processes – such as heuristic, collaborative, reflective, and analytical – can seamlessly coexist within increasingly open and digitally facilitated educational settings.\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe core idea behind the metasystem learning design is that learning outcomes arise from the interplay of various subsystems rather than from isolated teaching events. These subsystems generally encompass learners, educators, content, technological platforms, assessment tools, institutional policies, and wider sociocultural environments. As a result, learning is perceived as a process similar to an ecosystem, shaped by feedback loops, regulatory systems, and adaptive reactions over time [\u003Ca href=\"#B3\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E3\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E8\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. From this perspective, traditional linear instructional design models, characterized by fixed objectives, predetermined sequences, and standardized assessments, are insufficient for contemporary educational practice. The metasystem learning design emphasizes self-regulation, adaptability, and feedback diversity as its foundational principles. Rather than prescribing exact learning pathways, metasystem approaches aim to orchestrate environments in which learners can plan, monitor, and evaluate their learning strategies across contexts and modalities. A defining feature of metasystem learning ecosystems is the expanded role of feedback in the learning process [\u003Ca href=\"#B5\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E5\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B8\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E8\u003C\u002Fa\u003E]. Feedback is not limited to teacher comments on student work; it includes data-driven insights, peer interactions, self-assessments, and system-generated indicators such as learning analytics. When aligned with pedagogical intent, such feedback can support learner autonomy and reflective decision-making. However, metasystem theorists caution against allowing analytics or technological affordances to “drive the pedagogical bus,” warning that data collection without theoretical grounding risks reducing learning to what is most easily measurable rather than what is most educationally meaningful [\u003Ca href=\"#B12\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E12\u003C\u002Fa\u003E, \u003Ca href=\"#B16\" class=\"ref-link\" data-ref-style=\"bibr\"\u003E16\u003C\u002Fa\u003E].\u003C\u002Fp\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EDigital transformation plays a prominent role in the design of meta-system learning. Concepts such as digital micro-credentials, open badges, and modular learning pathways are framed as tools for recognizing learning in formal and informal contexts.
